ownership.value: Publicly traded on NYSE (CVNA) but a founder-controlled 'controlled company' with a dual-class share structure: the Garcia family controls roughly 85% of voting power through super-voting Class B shares; co-founder/CEO Ernie Garcia III is Chairman and CEO and his father Ernest Garcia II is the single largest individual shareholder (~7% economic stake) and controls related companies DriveTime and Bridgecrest; Vanguard and BlackRock are the largest institutional holders. No PE sponsor and no recent change of control.

debt_events.summary: Entered a $1.66 billion senior secured Term Loan B facility maturing 2033-08-14, priced at 99.75% of par, interest at Term SOFR+2.25% (or base rate+1.25%), 0.25% quarterly amortization, 50% excess-cash-flow sweep from FY2028, guaranteed by material domestic subsidiaries and secured by liens on substantially all collateral; the credit agreement has no financial covenant. Proceeds to redeem/refinance the 9.0%/11.0%/13.0% Cash/PIK Senior Secured Notes due 2030 — $1.0 billion redeemed 2026-08-15 and the remainder 2026-08-22 — replacing high-cost distress-era PIK paper with cheaper covenant-lite bank debt.

Transitioned to fully cash-paying interest in August 2025 (after ~$320M of non-cash PIK interest in the period ended 2026-06-30... i.e. period ended June 30, 2025); a $1.26 billion equity offering partially funded voluntary debt reduction; unrestricted cash was ~$1.86 billion at 2025-06-30; debt/EBITDA improved to ~3.2x for the 12 months ended 2025-06-30.

2023 out-of-court debt restructuring (context): exchange offers to swap 5.500% 2027, 5.875% 2028, 4.875% 2029 and 10.250% 2030 senior unsecured notes for up to $4.275 billion of new Cash/PIK senior secured notes due 2028/2030/2031, plus a $425.0 million cash tender offer for 5.625% 2025 notes at 85% of par, with consent solicitations stripping covenants; holders of more than 90% of unsecured notes had committed to participate.

credit_ratings.summary: Fitch Ratings assigned Carvana Co. a first-time Issuer Default Rating of 'BB-' with Outlook Stable (rating-action page: 'Fitch Assigns First-Time IDR of ‘BB-’ to Carvana Co.; Outlook Stable’).

Moody's upgraded Carvana's corporate family rating to B2 from B3 with a positive outlook; senior secured notes to B2 from B3 and senior unsecured notes to Caa1 from Caa2; cited improved operating performance, voluntary debt reduction, ~$985M LTM gains on receivables sales, debt/EBITDA ~3.2x, and noted good-liquidity assessment depends on continued ability to sell receivables for significant gains; further upgrades if debt/EBITDA below 4.0x and EBITDA-capex/interest above 3.0x.

Moody's upgraded Carvana's CFR to B3 from Caa1 (PDR to B3-PD, SGL to SGL-2) with positive outlook, citing improved operating performance and voluntary debt reduction; debt/EBITDA improved to ~4.2x at FYE2024 from ~18.8x at FYE2023.

S&P Global Ratings upgraded Carvana to 'B' from 'B-' (senior secured to 'B', senior unsecured to 'CCC+') with a positive outlook, citing improved performance and stronger credit metrics; a further upgrade possible within 12 months if leverage stays below 5x and FOCF/debt above 5%; company also has a $1 billion at-the-market equity facility after raising $1.3 billion via ATM in 2024 and redeeming $470 million of 2028 senior secured notes in 2024.

output.risk_rationale: Carvana's near-term credit risk is moderate and clearly improving rather than distressed: record Q2 2026 results (revenue $7,376M, +52% YoY; net income $513M; Adjusted EBITDA $769M), $2,630M of cash against $5,133M total debt at 2026-06-30 (net debt/TTM Adjusted EBITDA ~1.0x), and a string of upgrades — Moody's to B2/positive (Oct 2025), S&P to B/positive (Mar 2025) and a first-time Fitch 'BB-'/Stable (Jul 2026). In August 2026 it refinanced its high-cost 9.0%/11.0%/13.0% Cash/PIK 2030 notes with a $1.66B, seven-year, covenant-lite Term Loan B at SOFR+2.25%, eliminating PIK interest and extending maturity to 2033. Residual risk justifies staying at moderate rather than low: ratings remain high-yield single-B territory with Moody's flagging that good liquidity depends on continued gains from selling finance receivables, the Garcia family's ~85% voting control sits alongside extensive related-party dealings (DriveTime/Bridgecrest) that short sellers Gotham City Research (Jan 2026) and Hindenburg (Jan 2025) have attacked as accounting red flags, and consumer-protection enforcement (Connecticut's $1.5M settlement over title delays and late seller payments in Jan 2025) marks operational friction — though no covenant breach, missed payment, or going-concern language was found.

distress_signals.summary: Short seller Gotham City Research accused Carvana of overstating 2023-2024 earnings by more than $1 billion and of being 'far more dependent on related parties' (DriveTime and Bridgecrest, controlled by Ernest Garcia II) than disclosed, alleging earnings dependence on DriveTime's debt issuance and 'toxic' loans; CVNA shares fell 14.2% to $410.04, the second-worst trading day in a year. Carvana called the report 'inaccurate and intentionally misleading,' said all related-party transactions are accurately disclosed, and reconfirmed its Feb 18, 2026 earnings release date after Gotham claimed a 10-K delay was needed.

Heightened accounting scrutiny persisted into the Q4 2025 earnings call: CFO Mark Jenkins publicly refuted short-seller allegations of improper related-party disclosure as '100% inaccurate,' stressing there is 'no ambiguity' in Carvana's accounting practices. No CFO departure or auditor change reported; management stability maintained.

Hindenburg Research disclosed a short position in Carvana, claiming the turnaround was a 'mirage' propped up by unstable loans and accounting manipulation (referenced in CNBC's Jan 28, 2026 coverage of the Gotham City report).

Historical background only: during the 2022 downturn Carvana cut ~2,500 employees (~12% of workforce) and then a second round of ~1,500 (~8%) in November 2022 as used-car sales fell; no comparable restructuring actions found for 2025-2026.

payment_behaviour.summary: Connecticut Attorney General announced a $1.5 million settlement with Carvana after hundreds of consumer complaints: extended delays in title and registration documents, delayed payments to sellers and delayed loan payoffs (consumers forced to keep paying on vehicles no longer possessed), and misrepresentations of vehicle condition. Settlement set up a $1 million restitution fund plus a $500,000 penalty ($250,000 suspended on compliance); investigation opened January 2022; filed in Hartford Superior Court.
